skill.name: bevy-ecs-expert
skill.description: Master Bevy's Entity Component System (ECS) in Rust, covering Systems, Queries, Resources, and parallel scheduling.
skill.summary: Design efficient Bevy ECS components, systems, queries, resources, and schedules in Rust.
skill.author: sickn33

security_audit.summary: All 22 static findings are false positives caused by Rust syntax, Bevy ECS APIs, or Markdown backticks. The guide contains no executable scripts, shell commands, process launches, or prompt injection.

static_findings.snippet: Use simple structs for data. Derive `Component` and `Reflect`.
Use `Resource` for global data (score, game state).
Add systems to the `App` builder, defining execution order if needed.
Use `With` and `Without` to filter entities efficiently.
- ✅ **Do:** Use `Query` filters (`With`, `Without`, `Changed`) to reduce iteration count.
- ✅ **Do:** Prefer `Res` over `ResMut` when read-only access is sufficient to allow parallel executi
- ✅ **Do:** Use `Bundle` to spawn complex entities atomically.
- ❌ **Don't:** Use `RefCell` or interior mutability inside components; let the ECS handle borrowing.

content.value_statement: Bevy ECS design can create borrowing conflicts, slow queries, and unclear scheduling. This skill provides practical Rust patterns for components, systems, resources, filters, and ordering.
actual_capabilities: Defines data-oriented Bevy components with Component and Reflect derives.
Creates systems that query and update component data.
Models shared game state with Resource, Res, and ResMut.
Orders systems with schedules and chained execution.
Uses query filters to reduce unnecessary entity iteration.
Demonstrates entity spawning with required components and assets.
limitations: The examples may require changes for the Bevy version in your project.
The skill does not run, compile, benchmark, or test generated Rust code.
It covers core ECS patterns, not rendering, networking, physics, or deployment.
Project-specific architecture still requires profiling and validation.

use_cases.title: Structure a New Bevy Game
use_cases.description: Plan components, resources, systems, and schedules before implementing gameplay.
use_cases.target_user: Rust developers starting a Bevy project

use_cases.title: Resolve ECS Access Conflicts
use_cases.description: Review mutable access patterns and establish explicit system ordering.

use_cases.title: Optimize Entity Queries
use_cases.description: Apply filters and narrower access patterns to reduce work and improve parallel execution.

prompt_templates.title: Create a Component
prompt_templates.prompt: Create a Bevy component for [game concept]. Keep it data-oriented and explain each derive.

prompt_templates.title: Write a System
prompt_templates.prompt: Write a Bevy system that updates [component] using [resource]. Use the narrowest query and resource access possible.

prompt_templates.title: Fix a Query Conflict
prompt_templates.prompt: Review these Bevy systems for conflicting access: [systems]. Propose query filters, ParamSet, or scheduling changes and explain the tradeoffs.
prompt_templates.scenario: Debugging ECS borrowing or runtime conflicts

prompt_templates.title: Design an ECS Architecture
prompt_templates.prompt: Design the Bevy ECS architecture for [feature]. Define components, resources, events, systems, filters, schedules, ordering constraints, and performance risks.

output_examples.input: Design movement for player and enemy entities.
output: Use Velocity as a component containing movement data.
Query Transform and Velocity, then filter player and enemy behavior separately.
Read Time as an immutable resource to preserve parallel scheduling.

output_examples.input: Two systems need mutable access to the same component.
output_examples.output: The systems cannot run in parallel with overlapping mutable access. Chain them when order matters, or partition entities with disjoint query filters.

output_examples.input: Improve a query that scans every entity each frame.
output_examples.output: Add With, Without, or Changed filters that match the gameplay condition. Keep query data narrow and confirm the improvement with profiling.

best_practices: Keep components focused on data and place behavior in systems.
Prefer immutable resource access when mutation is unnecessary.
Profile representative workloads before changing ECS architecture.
anti_patterns: Do not store unrelated global state in one large resource.
Do not use broad mutable queries when filters can separate entity sets.
Do not force system ordering unless data dependencies require it.

faq.question: Which Bevy topics does this skill cover?
faq.answer: It covers components, systems, queries, resources, entity spawning, filters, scheduling, and parallel access patterns.

faq.question: Does it support every Bevy version?
faq.answer: No. Bevy APIs change, so verify examples against your project's dependency version.

faq.question: Can it diagnose mutable access conflicts?
faq.answer: It can identify likely conflicts and suggest filters or ordering. You must validate the result in your application.

faq.question: Can it optimize performance automatically?
faq.answer: No. It suggests ECS patterns, but reliable optimization requires measurements from representative gameplay.

faq.question: Does it generate complete games?
faq.answer: No. It focuses on ECS architecture and small Rust examples for specific gameplay systems.

faq.question: Does it execute commands or scripts?
faq.answer: No. The skill is a documentation guide and contains only Markdown prose and Rust examples.
